chunks.heading: Chapter 11 288
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 288
Working through this chapter gave you a complete end-to-end implementation of a regulated
AI assistant connected to live structured data. The patterns applied here — identity-gated data
retrieval, compliance blocklists, High groundedness thresholds, and mandatory pre-
deployment evaluation — are directly transferable to other regulated domains such as
insurance, healthcare, and legal services. In the next chapter, you will explore how to extend
these patterns to multi-agent architectures, where multiple specialized agents collaborate
within a single Microsoft Foundry project.
Performance at scale
Production deployment with thousands of concurrent customers introduces three critical
operational challenges: unpredictable latency degradation as identity verification, security
checks, and Fabric queries contend for shared resources; schema changes in Fabric that break
agent behavior when field names or data structures evolve; and the difficulty of maintaining
compliance guardrails while scaling data access patterns. This section addresses these
production realities specific to the Foundry agent deployment model.
Reducing latency under customer traffic
When deployed in Foundry, the idx_649e8d3fidx_eae60aac agent processes each query sequentially through identity
verification → scope validation → row-level security check → Fabric query → guardrail
evaluation. In single-customer tests, this completes in 1–2 seconds. At scale (100+ concurrent
requests), contention for the Fabric capacity and guardrail evaluation bottlenecks latency to 5–
10 seconds.
Consider the following recommendations as part of the actions you can take to impact latency:
Model deployment scaling in Discover tab: In Discover → Models, the gpt-4.1-
banking model deployment includes a Tokens per Minute (TPM) setting. Under
heavy traffic, increase the TPM limit from 50K to 100K or higher (according to your
Azure quota). This allows the model to process more concurrent requests without
queuing delays. Monitor via Operate → Monitoring to track if you're hitting TPM
limits during peak hours.
Use Foundry's built-in request prioritization: In Build → Agents, open the agent
settings and enable Request prioritization (if available in your Foundry version). This
routes simple queries (e.g., "What is my balance?") faster than complex multi-turn
conversations, reducing perceived latency for the majority of users.
Enable agent caching in Build → Agents settings: Foundry agents support response
caching. In the agent's Settings panel, enable Cache responses with a 10-minute TTL.
Identical queries from the same customer within 10 minutes return cached results
•
•
•

immediately (50–70% reduction in Fabric query overhead). Monitor cache hit rates in

Operate → Monitoring.
Optimize Knowledge source queries in Build: In Build → Agents → Knowledge
section, the Fabric connector routing instructions in the system prompt directly affect
query complexity. Refactor instructions to use simpler natural language queries:
instead of "Return all transactions for account X from date Y to Z with merchant
categories", use "Show recent transactions for account X." Foundry will interpret the
simpler query with less overhead.
Connection pooling validation in Management Center: In Build → Agents, open
the Fabric connection details (Connected resources in Management Center). Confirm
that the connection is configured with Azure connection pooling enabled. This reduces
idx_8256276eidx_abde1197 per-query connection overhead by reusing TCP connections to Fabric.
Managing schema changes without breaking the agent
When Fabric data engineers idx_3eb10e34idx_ff3d954d add fields (e.g., loyalty_points_balance) or rename columns
(CurrentBalance to AvailableBalance), the agent's system prompt and Knowledge source
routing may hardcode field names. If fields are missing or renamed, the agent hallucinates or
returns errors, causing customer-facing failures.
Consider the following recommendations as part of the actions you can take to avoid failures
due to schema changes:
Version your Fabric connections in Management Center: Do not modify the existing
Fabric connection in place. In Build → Agents → Connected resources, create new
versions: banking ‑ fabric ‑ v1, banking ‑ fabric ‑ v2. When Fabric schema changes,
create a new connection pointing to the updated schema. In the agent's Build settings,
you can test against the new connection in a staging environment before switching
production agents.
Use Foundry's schema inspection in the agent editor: In Build → Agents, scroll to
the Knowledge section and click the Fabric connection. Foundry displays the
available fields and data types returned by the Fabric Data Agent. Before deploying any
agent changes, verify that all required fields are present. If a field is missing, contact the
Fabric team and block agent deployment until the field is available.
Document field requirements in the system prompt: In Build → Agents →
Instructions, add a field manifest:
Required Fabric fields: account_number, balance, account_type, status If
any required field is missing from the result, respond:
"I was unable to retrieve complete account information. Please try again

the agent never processes incomplete data from Fabric.
Compliance at scale
As customer traffic idx_2a3ba60bidx_38d04e67 increases, monitoring guardrail effectiveness—sensitive data protection,
groundedness, blocklist hits, identity verification—becomes critical. Silent failures
(groundedness drift, guardrail bypasses) are dangerous in regulated banking environments.
Consider the following recommendations as part of the actions you can take to keep your agent
solution in compliance:
Monitor guardrail effectiveness in Operate → Monitoring: Foundry dashboards
display:
Guardrail annotation rate by control: Track the percentage of requests hitting
each control (content harm, prompt injection, sensitive data, blocklist, etc.). If
prompt injection blocks jump above 5% of traffic, investigate for attack patterns.
If sensitive data detection spikes, review for field exposure issues.
Task adherence scores: Monitor the percentage of responses that follow system
prompt rules. If task adherence drops below 4.5/5, schema changes or prompt
drift may be occurring.
Groundedness scores: Track how many responses are fully traceable to Fabric
results. If groundedness drops below 4.5/5, the agent may be hallucinating due to

Full conversation flow (customer query, agent reasoning, Fabric call, response)

Also, the evaluation dataset covered twelve scenarios with the strictest thresholds of the three

Building an Agent that Uses

In this final chapter, we will build another real-world use case directly in the Microsoft
Foundry new portal. The idx_9f88e629 objective is clear: create a conversational Agent capable of answering
customer questions about their retail activity and loyalty points, while securely retrieving
personalized data from a Databricks Genie exposed through MCP. Instead of focusing on
code, we will prioritize configuration inside the portal — where you click, what you configure,
and why each decision matters.
This scenario reflects a common business requirement: blending conversational AI with
trusted enterprise data. The Agent must know when to answer from its general instructions
and when to call an external system for customer-specific information. That means defining
clear behavior, connecting tools properly, and ensuring that responses are accurate, safe, and
grounded in real data. The integration with Databricks Genie enables the Agent to retrieve
structured information, such as purchase history and accumulated points, without embedding
that data directly into the model.
By the end of this chapter, you will have configured an agent that can intelligently route
customer queries to Genie through MCP, shape the response appropriately, and handle
missing or incomplete information gracefully. Everything will be built step by step in the
Microsoft Foundry portal, following the same UI approach used earlier, so you can replicate
this pattern in your own production scenarios.
We will cover these under the following main headings:
Scope and assumptions for the use case

Technical requirements
Before starting this chapter, confirm the following are in place: An active Azure subscription
with Contributor rights on a resource group, an Azure Databricks workspace with Managed
MCP Servers enabled and at least one published Genie space covering retail customer data
(purchase history and loyalty points), GPT-4.1 quota available in the target Azure region, and

Scope and assumptions of the use case

Before we idx_40d1d135 start clicking through the Microsoft Foundry portal, we need to clearly define what
this agent is responsible for — and just as importantly, what it is not responsible for. A well-
defined scope is what keeps an AI solution reliable, secure, and predictable in production.
For this chapter, we will build a customer-facing support agent that answers questions related
to retail store activity and loyalty points. The agent must be able to respond to general
questions conversationally, but whenever a customer asks about their personal activity, it
must retrieve information from a Databricks Genie exposed through MCP. The agent itself does
not store purchase history or loyalty data — it only queries Genie when needed.
Let's define the scope more precisely.
In-scope scenarios
The agent idx_87cb2195 should support the following types of requests:
"How many loyalty points do I currently have?"
"What were my last three purchases?"
"Show me what I bought last month"
"When were my loyalty points last updated?"
"What is the total amount I spent this year?"

Chapter 12 296
These scenarios all share a common characteristic: they require customer-specific data. That
means the Agent must call the MCP-connected Databricks Genie tool to retrieve structured
information such as:
Points balance
Points transaction history
Purchase summaries
Purchase date ranges
Totals per period
The agent may also receive hybrid questions, such as, "How do I earn points, and how many do
I have right now?"
In this case, the first part ("How do I earn points?") can be answered from the agent's
instructions or knowledge base, while the second part requires a Genie call. The agent must
handle this combination intelligently.
Required inputs and identity assumptions
Because idx_2030acea this solution involves personal customer data, we idx_8486fc7d must define how identity is
handled.
For this chapter, we assume:
The customer provides an accepted identifier (for example, loyalty ID or registered
email)
The agent is allowed to pass this identifier to Genie via MCP
Genie returns only the data fields configured in its exposed schema
The Agent must:
Ask for an identifier if it is missing
Avoid guessing or fabricating customer data
Clearly state when no data is found
For example, if a customer asks, "How many points do I have?", and no identifier is present, the
agent should respond: "To check your loyalty points, I'll need your loyalty ID or registered
email."
This behavior will later be enforced in the Agent's instructions and tool configuration.
Data exposure principles
Since idx_d7428cae we are integrating enterprise data, we must follow a "minimum necessary" principle.

That means:
If the customer asks for points balance, return the balance — not their entire purchase
history
If they ask for the last three purchases, return a summary (date, total, category), not
every internal column
If a large dataset is returned, summarize it conversationally
Success criteria
By the end idx_ba230ea1 of this chapter, the agent should:
Correctly detect when a question requires Genie data
Request a customer identifier if it is missing
Call the MCP -connected Genie tool with the proper parameters
Format the response clearly and safely
Handle cases where:
No data exists
Partial data is returned
The tool call fails
If those conditions are met, the agent is behaving as designed.

Chapter 12 298
Figure 12.1: Request Lifecycle and Trust Boundaries
Let's idx_c4002393 break down these steps:
Step 1 — Customer sends query (Teams/Copilot): Query reaches the Foundry agent
endpoint as plain text.
Step 2 — System Prompt evaluates routing: The prompt decides: does this require
Genie data? " How do I earn points? " = no. " What's my balance? " = yes. This is the
tool router decision.
Step 3 — Guardrails validate input: Security checks block prompt injection, abusive
content, and out-of-scope requests before the model processes them.
Step 4 — Prepare MCP Request + Authenticate (parallel): The SDK packages the
Genie query. Simultaneously, Microsoft Entra ID authenticates the agent's managed
identity (not your credentials — the agent's system-assigned service principal). This
identity is the only one allowed to call Databricks at runtime.
Steps 5-6 — MCP Protocol sends request to Databricks: The authenticated request
travels through MCP (JSON-RPC), which acts as an abstraction layer. If Databricks
changes its schema, MCP absorbs the change — Foundry doesn't break. Genie executes
the query against customer data within row-level security boundaries.
Step 7 — Return Structured Data: Databricks returns the full dataset (maybe 20
fields, 50 rows) through MCP back to Foundry.
Step 8 — Format Response and Data Minimization: The agent extracts only relevant
fields. Customer asks, " What's my balance? ", and the agent returns the number and
timestamp, not the entire purchase history. Data minimization prevents accidental
information exposure.

All steps are idx_1a1bc93c logged to Application Insights for full auditability. With this lifecycle understood,
each configuration step that follows has a clear purpose: system prompt controls behavior,
guardrails enforce it, Managed Identity ensures security, MCP isolates from Databricks
internals, data minimization protects privacy, and logging enables production visibility.
Let's test this architecture with an example to understand how this will work before starting to
create and deploy components, a customer query end-to-end.
To make the 8-step flow concrete, trace a real customer interaction through the system:
The customer asks: "Hi, I have loyalty ID 10045. What were my last three purchases and how
many points do I have?"
Step 1 — Query reaches agent: " Hi, I have loyalty ID 10045. What were my
last three purchases and how many points do I have? " is sent to the Foundry
agent endpoint.
Step 2 — System Prompt routes: The prompt evaluates the question. It contains
personal data requests (purchases, points), so a Genie call is required. The prompt also
identifies that the loyalty ID is present, so no escalation for missing identity is needed.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 298
chunks.content:
Step 3 — Guardrails validate: Input checks run. No prompt injection detected. No
abusive content. Not an out-of-scope request like "process a refund." Input passes
validation and continues.
Step 4 — Prepare request + authenticate: The Foundry SDK packages the query as a
natural idx_3ab55790 language request: " Show the last three purchases and current points
balance for loyalty ID 10045. " Simultaneously, Entra ID authenticates the agent's
managed identity and returns a valid token.
Steps 5-6 — MCP protocol + Databricks execute: The authenticated request travels
through MCP to Databricks. Genie receives the query, checks row-level security
(verified: this managed identity can access data for loyalty ID 10045), executes the
query against the Genie space, and returns the result.
Genie's response (simplified):

"Groceries"}], "points_balance": 2847, "last_updated":

Step 7 — Return data: The full dataset arrives back at Foundry through MCP.
Step 8 — Format and minimize: The agent receives all the data but applies data
minimization. The system prompt said: " Only return data fields directly
relevant to the customer's question. Do not paste raw data. "
The agent's response to the customer:
"Great! Here's what I found for loyalty ID 10045:
Recent purchases:
May 15: Electronics ($87.50)
May 10: Clothing ($42.30)
Apr 28: Groceries ($156.99)
Loyalty points: You have 2,847 points. Last updated May 15."
Now, let's try to idx_2aaeaf19 understand what happened here:
What the customer sees: A clean, conversational response with exactly the
information requested. No raw JSON. No internal field names. No data they didn't ask
for.
What happens in the background (logged to Application Insights): Every step is
recorded — validation result, tool call timestamp, Genie response size (in this case,
~400 tokens), response latency (in this case, 1.8 seconds), data minimization applied,
and the final response delivered. If the customer later disputes what they were told,
this audit trail shows exactly what happened.
What happens if something breaks: If the Genie space was unavailable during Step 6,
the agent responds with " I'm having trouble retrieving that information
right now. Please try again in a moment or contact support. " The error is
logged. Your monitoring alerts fire (tool success rate dropped below 95%). You have 15
minutes to investigate and fix before the SLA is breached.
With this end-to-end flow in mind, the configuration steps that follow make more sense.
